results.title: Salima Ikram: The Animal Mummy Project
results.description: Professor Salima Ikram is the world's leading expert on animal mummies and founder of the Animal Mummy project at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. She is the author of several books on Egyptian archaeology and is a leading scholars in Egyptian funerary archaeology. She says despite the fact that animal mummies were not valued as artifacts, many have survived, which teaches us a huge amount about the culture and environment of ancient Egypt. She even teaches people how to mummify animals.

results.fulltext: the manufacture of mummies mummy restoration is the newest of the arts having been invented recently by a scientist connected with the american museum of natural history in jntew york by the aid of a simple yet ingenious process it brings back the ancient dead to the aspect of life or something near it giving them the appearance they had hundreds or even thousands of years ago mummification consists of course in the withdrawal of all water from the tissues of the body which is thus reduced to absolute dryness it follows then that if the water can be putback into the flesh and parchment-like skin the desiccated individual will be restored to something like his original appearance this is exactly what is accomplished by the process referred to the desiccation is so absolute that the body of a man who weighed perhaps iso pounds in jife is likely to tip the scales at not more than fourteen pounds all of the tissues being extremely shrunken while the parchment-like skin holds the bones like a bag as a rule the hair is well preserved and in many instances the eyes are quite perfect yet in many cases doubtless the mummies are thousands of years old the process of restoration consists in placing the munimj in ai box and introducing water vapour in the shape of comparatively cool steam it has to be done gradually but when properly applied the vapour is slowly absorbed the dried body finally assuming the contour of life from a scientific standpoint the achievement is most interesting inasmuch as the ethnologist is enabled to ascertain what these mummied people looked like when they were alive i when thus restored the mummies become liable to decay and for that reason they are preserved in alcohol the manufacture of artificial mummies a very different process from the foregoing has recently become quite a profitable industry out of a consignment of twenty-one mummies shipped not long ago froim egypt to an institution in america by a well-known archaeologist nineteen were found to be frauds skeletons obtained by professional ghoula from modern graveyards are wrapped in a kind of cloth resembling in appearance the mummy-cloth of the ancient egyptians the wrapping is done with the help of modern glue and when the mummy is finished it is placed in a counterfeit mummy-coffin of papier mache mummy-coffins of this kind are being turned out by hundreds in paris painted from egyptian originals with the curious and complicated figures and inscriptions customarily applied to such boxes for the dead in the days of the pharaohs finally the imitation mummies enclosed in the bogus cases are shipped to egypt where they are sold to tourists at profitable rates a mummy in good condition is worth from 15 to 100 it is a curious fact that frauds in mummies were commonly practised in ancient egypt all of the business of mummy-making was in the hands of the priests and it was part of their work to preserve in this way the bodies of sacred animals such as cats crocodiles and ibises frequently however they preferred to do up a bundle of rags and palm it off as the mummy of a monkey or an ibis getting their pay just the same doubtless so common was this practice that nowadays mummies of animals received from egypt are x-rayed before taking the trouble to unwrap them fake mummies are by no means unknown in america only a short time ago the alleged mummy of a nine-foot giant turned up in atlanta having been found so the showman said who owed it in california it was so excellently made as to deceive some expert archaeologists and the fact that it was counterfeit might never biave been discovered had it not been that the proprietor was arrested for debt meanwhile mr f a lucas of thcs smithsonian institution results.title: Egypt unveils ancient female sarcophagus dating back to 3000 years
results.description: A well-preserved mummy of a woman inside a previously unopened coffin dating back to more than 3000 years has been unveiled in Egypt.
results.fulltext: Egyptian authorities unveiled a well-preserved mummy of a woman inside a previously unopened coffin in Luxor in southern Egypt dating back to more than 3000 years. The sarcophagus, an ancient coffin, was one of two found earlier this month by a French-led mission in the northern area of El-Asasif, a necropolis on the western bank of the Nile. The first one had been opened earlier and examined by Egyptian antiquities officials. "One sarcophagus was rishi-style, which dates back to the 17th dynasty, while the other sarcophagus was from the 18th dynasty," Minister of Antiquities Khaled Al Anani said. "The two tombs were present with their mummies inside." The 18th dynasty dates back to the 13th century BC, a period noted for some of the most well known Pharaohs, including Tutankhamen and Ramses II0. It was the first known time that authorities had opened a previously unopened sarcophagus before international media. Earlier in the day, authorities also revealed in the same area the tomb of the overseer of the mummification shrine identified as Thaw-Irkhet-if. The tomb contained five coloured masks and some 1000 Ushabti statutes - the miniature figurine of servants to serve the dead in the afterlife. Three-hundred cubic metres of rubble were removed over five months to uncover the tomb, which contained coloured ceiling paintings depicting the owner and his family. The tomb, which also contains mummies, skeletons and skulls, dates back to the middle-kingdom almost 4000 years ago, but was reused during the late period. Ancient Egyptians mummified humans to preserve their bodies for the afterlife, while animal mummies were used as religious offerings. Egypt has revealed over a dozen ancient discoveries since the beginning of this year. The country hopes these discoveries will brighten its image abroad and revive interest among travellers who once flocked to its iconic pharaonic temples and pyramids but who have shunned the country since its 2011 political uprising. - Reuters

results.fulltext: some american mummies the history of embalming in egypt is well known and it is a more or less interesting study to attempt to compare the making of mummies in the east ana in america with a view to throwing light on the singularities and religious observances which formed a part of the ceremony of mummification from a translation of sepulchural texts in egypt it has been learned that mummies were made there to keep the body inviolate and ready for the return of the soul at the time of resurrection the egyptians seemed to recognise four parts in a man the body the soul an intelligence and an appearance eidolon at death these were separated and then inter-1 vened a period of from three thousand to ten thousand years during this time the soul travelled the under-world as a penance while the intellirnce wandered through space as these parts were to return at the end of the time indicated it was considered necessary to preserve the body from corruption and in the attempts to accomplish this we find the reason for embalming among the ancient egyptians their pyramids their secret burials ana the extraordinary methods of hiding the dead customs which have been of the greatest value to archaeologists and students of man and the human race the embalming process was carried on with greater or less ceremony and expense in proportion to the wealth of the deceased and if the latter were a king or a member of the roya family or a wealthy man no expense was spared to embalm him in a lasting manner and to place the remains in a well built tomb the embalming was carried out on a regular system there being four rituals to grovern it the first related to the incisions to be made in the body the second was a manual treating of the gums resins and spices to be used the bandages and elaborate descriptions as to the method of binding the body and the prayers u be recited at each stage of the work third the water ritual giving the litanies to be recited while the body was being taken by water to its last resting place and fourth the work containing the funeral ritual given when the body was placed in the tomb these books were for the instruction of the priests and operators the drqcess of embalming was divided first came the evisceration taking about two weeks this was followed by the salting or bituminising which took 30 days then came the spicing and bandaging occupying 35 days or 72 days in all the great cemeteries of these days all had establishments fob making mummies attached to them as crematories are found to-day and the professional embalmers constituted an army of people in themselves according to edwards there were never less than 800 bodies in process of mummification in the work-shops of the necropolis of memphis the method of treatment depended upon the rank and wealth of the dead in the case of a poor man the bandages would be coarse but if the deceased was wealthy they were of the finest linen each finder and limb were bound 1250 yards having in some cases been enrolled by investigatorsnearly two tfrirds of a mile of bandages 3in or 4in in width there were many methods of making mummies and time has shown that those of the theban epoch were the best the bodies after centuries being so flexible that they can be bent without breaking this was it is supposed due to the expensive ingredients employed mummies of some kind are found in 1 many lands and it is interesting to note that they occur in-various parts of the united states possibly the most interesting coming from the caves of arizona according to lawson the santee indians of south carolina preserved their dead by embalming with certain roots after which they dried the body and covered it with the bark of the pine or cypress finally the skeleton was secured and wrapped in cloth made of opossum hair the remains being placed in a box others are wrapped in deerskins and stored in the quiogozon which was the royal tomb perfect mummies have been found in the caves of kentucky one enveloped in rough clothes and wrapped in deerskins was found ten feet below the surface in a cave it was the bodyof a woman the hair shaven off according to custom beneath the outer deerskin was another skin of the deer then came a clotn formed of twine inside of this was a cloth resembling this but covered and ornamented with brown feathers the natives of the northt-welit embalmed their dead the body was usually doubled up and placed in a case of fur or grass made for the purpose the alaskan commercial company secured from the seal islands of the company a mummy supposed to be 150 years old which shows that this method of burial has been followed for many years it was discovered on a cave in kagamale island filled with sulphurous vapours which came from crevices in the rock eleven mummies were found one the chief was held by a basket like coffin or structure 4ft in height and evidently made with the greatest care the material with which the remains were wrapped were matting woven from seaweed in a very skilful manner and1 skins amongl which was a fine skin of the sea otter over all was a net made of the sinews of the sea lion in many of the so-called-mummies of america the body was placed in a sitting position several were found by the writer on san clemente island california doubled up the head resting on the knees while in front of the face and behind the head were placed flutes of bone inlaid with the pearly abalone the so-called mummy caves of arizona from which mummies have been taken are very interesting results.fulltext: evening post saturday february 17 1923 after three thousand years the furthest limit of barbarity and callousness of which a civilised age was capable in its treatment of the dead seemed to have been reached by the germans during the war when the times published a facsimile of an army order relating to the management of corpse utilisation establishments the requirement that when bodiesvwere sent to these establishments returns as to the unit date of death illness and information as to contagious diseases if any are to be furnished at the same time appeared to confirm the belief that it was not to the bodies of dead animals that these regulations related it looked as though the corpses of the soldiers who had already served as fodder for the cannon of the enemy were being used by the ruthless economy of the germans to feed their own guns after transmutation into lubricants or ingredients in high explosives or other warlike material hamlet imagined that imperious caesar dead and turned to clay might stop a hole to keep the wind away and that the dust of alexander might serve to stop a beer-barrel why should not the circuitous and tedious processes of nature be hastened and directed in a utilitarian age by the shortest cut known to the scientific barbarians of germany and the soldier who fell in the firing line yesterday made to continue his service against the enemy to-day in the form of ammunition at this time of day it is preferable to think that the times was hoaxed and that nothing but the fact that we were all seeing red prevented us from perceiving it but the imaginary horror may nevertheless serve as a foil to an example of the opposite kind which was reported a few days ago if the procedure attributed to the germans represented the furthest limit of callousness in the treatment of the dead sir rider haggard plea for tutankhamen surely carries sentiment just as far as it will go in the opposite dis-ection after the lapse of three thousand years the body of tutankhamen is to be restored to-morrow to the light of day the public is not yet so deeply absorbed by the duke of york wedding that it cannot spare a thought for this infinitely more remarkable event but sir rider haggard is very anxious that after the public curiosity has been satisfied and science has made all the obser j vations and records that it needs the egyptian king shall be withdrawn from the vulgar gaze and allowed to resume his sleep unmolested in a letter to the times of which a summary was cabled to us on wednesday he suggests that after a necessary x-ray investigation and the making of wax models tutankhamen mummy should be sealed up in a chamber of the great pyramid in such a fashion that only the complete destruction of the pyramid would reveal it sir rider haggard displays an honourable tenderness of feeling and his conclusion mas be correct but some of the arguments by which he supports it offer an easy opening for attack and raise some very interesting ooints of casuistry the relics of people he ea-ys who in their way were great as we are and certainly mere religious should be sacred it is indecent and unlicly to put mummies of kings in a glass case in the cairo museum to rot end become a inervy jest for tourists the greatest horror by which the pharaohs were obsc-sed was the fear of the desecration of their tombs another of their obsessions was the fear that they might not have enough food clothing and other articles of necessity or luxury to carry them safely through their long journey to the other world are we therefore to respect the provision which they made for themselves thousands of years ago and instead of jealously guarding what is left in our museums and making it the vehicle of instruction acd pleasure to thousands to put it underground again and perhaps make some addition to the equipment it is clear that we cannot reasonably treat the superstitious beliefs and the impossible desires of these ancient kings as binding upon us for all time nor does sir eider haggard argue that we should so treat them it is only the person of tutankhamenor what was so regarded in lifeand not the apparatus which ho considered to be just as necessary for his salvation as the preservation of his corpse that sir rider haggard asks to treat as still subject to the wishes of the proprietor of three thousand years ago when sir rider haggard says that it is indecent and unholy to put mummies of great kings in a glass case in the cairo museum to rot and becom a merry jest for tourists he seems to fall into at least three fallacies in the first place he pleads only for the mummies of great kings but surely not royalty but humanity is the only safe ground to take is not the unknown soldier entitled to just the same protection as imperious caesar himself 1 secondly if the mummy goes to the cairo museum it will not be to rot but to be faithfully preserved by the care of science thirdly it is absurd to suggest that it would there serve as a mei-ry jest for tourists there is indeed nothing as an old writer says of a majesty so sacred but that an itching tongue may rub itself thereon but the mummy of the supposed pharaoh of the exodus which is already in the cairo museum serves a higher purpose than that of a butt for vulgar humour and so would the mummy of tutankhamen sir rider haggard says that the ancient egyptians were in their way as great as we are and certainly more religious if they were not a great people they certainly had great tyrants and if the tomb to which sir rider haggard proposes to consign tutankhamen has no lofty religious associations it may nevertheless be well suited for the purpose of the king who built the great pyramid herodotus says he closed the temples and forbade the egyptians to offer sacrifice compelling them instead to labour one and all in his service a hundred thousand men laboured constantly and were relieved every three months by a fresh lot it took ten years of oppression to make the causeway for the conveyance of the stones the pyramid itself was twenty years in building a pyramid which was built in this way may perhaps be a fitter restingplace for tutankhamen than the cairo museum but sir rider haggard had better leave the religion out of it

results.fulltext:
This fragment of a shroud or mummy wrapping is made of finely woven pale brown linen, and dates to the early Ptolemaic period around 300 BC. Depicted on the linen are scenes from the Book of the Dead, showing a funeral procession. Beneath the funeral scene is an inscription, with the text written in Egyptian hieratic.

The illustration, from left to right, includes: butchers cutting up an ox as an offering; men carrying furniture for the after-life; four standard bearers with nome signs (hawk, ibis and jackals); a funerary boat with the figures of Isis and Nepthys on either side; and a man pulling a sledge bearing an image of Anubis, Protector of the Dead.

A similar scene occurs at the beginning of the copy of the Book of the Dead on the Turin Papyrus.

results.title: Mitogenomic diversity in Sacred Ibis Mummies sheds light on early Egyptian practices.
results.description: The ancient catacombs of Egypt harbor millions of well-preserved mummified Sacred Ibis (Threskiornis aethiopicus) dating from ~600BC. Although it is known that a very large number of these 'votive' mummies were sacrificed to the Egyptian God Thoth, how the ancient Egyptians obtained millions of these birds for mummification remains unresolved. Ancient Egyptian textual evidences suggest they may have been raised in dedicated large-scale farms. To investigate the most likely method used by the priests to secure birds for mummification, we report the first study of complete mitochondrial genomes of 14 Sacred Ibis mummies interred ~2500 years ago. We analysed and compared the mitogenomic diversity among Sacred Ibis mummies to that found in modern Sacred Ibis populations from throughout Africa. The ancient birds show a high level of genetic variation comparable to that identified in modern African populations, contrary to the suggestion in ancient hieroglyphics (or ancient writings) of centralized industrial scale farming of sacrificial birds. This suggests a sustained short-term taming of the wild migratory Sacred Ibis for the ritual yearly demand

results.fulltext:
This resin copy of an Egyptian scarab beetle features a hieroglyphic inscription on the base. 

The Egyptians saw the scarab as a symbol of renewal and rebirth. Scarab beetles were linked with the sun god Ra, particularly through his personification as Khepri. Scarab beetles are known for the balls of dung they lay their eggs in which was a symbol of the full circle of life and rebirth.

Scarabs were popular amulets and a sign of protection and good luck. Commonly made of stone, the carving was often both an adult and a seal. Inscriptions on the base could range from spiral motifs to official titles to complete mottoes and excerpts from the Book of the Dead. 

The amulets were also revered for their magical properties of rejuvenation, for both the living and the deceased. From the time of the New Kingdom (1539-1075 BCE), amulets of scarabs were placed with mummies. Initially they were solely placed on the chest, over time this grew to placing several around the body. When placed on the chest, they symbolised the heart of the deceased.Hieroglyphs on base

results.fulltext: THE BLOOD TEST. CRIMINALS, BEWARE! AN INFALLIBLE METHOD. BY ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH.—COPYRIGHT. ' Plilt UNITED I'KESS ASSOCIATION. Received February 15, 9.35 a m LONDON, Feb.' 14. A demonstration at the Royal Instituete of Public Health of the serological test infallibly distinguished various mammalian bloods. The wrappings of an Egyptian mummy also responded to the test. This method has been utilised in the Clapham Common murder. The "new scrum test," used for the first time in a recent English criminal case, is an application of one of the most remarkable discoveries in physiological chemistry. It depends upon the discovery that the serum from a rabbit or mouse into which human serum had been injected gave a precipitate with the serum of human blood, but not with that from the blood of animals. Even blood stains several months old, when dissolved in a dilute solution of sodium chloride, gave the reaction, though a stain nine years old failed to react. The first occasion upon which this test was employed in criminal work was in the trial that took place in France some five years ago. The prisoner had stated that a blood stain had been caused by the blood of a rabbit. A serum specific for rabbit's blood serum was therefore prepared, and when this gave no precipitate within thirty minutes -with an extract from the stain it could be stated with certainty that no rabbit's blood was present. At the inquest on Beron, who was murdered at Clapham Common, a verdicet of wilful murder was returned against Morrison, who is under arrest charged with the crime.
